produced_by: claude-fable-5-1 labellers working in parallel from reference/labelling-brief.txt, each shown the review text alone
notes: No Man's Sky. Labelled from snapshot=1788877626, which holds 415,104 of the 415,129 reviews Valve reports (99.99%), across 16 date shards.

Drawn by `census sample 296970 3551340 548430 275850 1091500 553850 --out data --random 100 --per-category 40 --seed 1 --brief --batch-size 35`. The stratified subset is pooled across all six games, so a category one game barely discusses is supplied by a game that does. The same seed against the same capture draws the same reviews, which is why sample.json need not be kept.

249 labels: 149 stratified and 100 random. The two subsets have different jobs and must not be merged. The stratified labels are TRAINING DATA, so any figure measured over them says what the anchors memorised. The random labels are held back from fitting entirely and are the only ones that measure anything.

Labellers were given the review text and the category sheet, never the classifier's prediction. Agreement measured against this set is therefore not inflated by labellers anchoring on the guess they are being compared against.

53 of the 249 labels (21.3%) are flagged ambiguous, the lowest share of the six sets. Reviews of this game tend to name a specific subject rather than deliver a bare verdict, which is what makes them easy to place.

The only game of the six whose reviews touch all 21 categories, both as a primary label and as a mention. Nine years of free updates that turned a badly received launch around gives it an unusually wide spread: `updates` is its largest category, and its reviews argue about the launch, the redemption and the game itself in the same paragraph.

Measured with anchors pooled from all six sets: 56.0% primary agreement on the held-out random subset [46.2, 65.3], macro F1 0.497, the best of the six. Split by how the labeller called it, 60.0% on the 75 clear-cut reviews and 44.0% on the 25 contested ones. `updates` reaches F1 0.76 on 84 reference mentions, the strongest showing any category makes anywhere in the set.
Anchors fitted on the other five games and never on this one reach 51.0% against 32.0% for the written descriptions: 31 reviews move to the right category and 12 move away.

Pooled over all six held-out random subsets, 600 reviews in total: written descriptions agree with the labels on 30.0%, anchors fitted on the five other games on 46.3%, and anchors fitted on all six on 52.7%. Of the 242 reviews the descriptions and the unseen-game fit place differently, 170 move to the category the labels give and 72 move away (exact McNemar p < 0.0001). Labels from other games are therefore worth about 16 points, and labelling the game itself a further 6. Split by how the labeller called it, the pooled figure is 62.1% on the 435 clear-cut reviews and 27.9% on the 165 contested ones. Reproduce with `census fit 296970 3551340 548430 275850 1091500 553850 --out data --leave-one-out`.

Because no person has checked these labels, results measured against this set are AGREEMENT WITH A MODEL and must never be reported as accuracy. Two language models agreeing can be wrong together, and the sarcasm and boundary cases where this classifier is weakest are exactly where that correlation is strongest. Set human_verified to true only once a person has labelled a subset independently, and record how large that subset was.

Taxonomy gaps the labellers reported, worth weighing before any future spine: tutorial and onboarding quality, asked for by three separate labellers and currently split between gameplay and difficulty; co-op as a genre trait rather than a multiplayer feature; real-world licensing with no home of its own; VR support and immersion, which this game raises more than any other; and protests that name a publisher but no requirement, which the offtopic boundary sends to offtopic.
